content: Allergy is a condition of the immune system, often referred to as atopy. It involves hypersensitivity reactions to environmental substances known as allergens. These reactions are acquired, predictable, and occur rapidly. Allergy is classified as one of the four types of hypersensitivity, specifically Type I hypersensitivity, also known as immediate hypersensitivity. This condition is characterized by the overactivation of specific white blood cells, namely mast cells and basophils, through the action of an antibody called immunoglobulin E (IgE). This process leads to an exaggerated inflammatory response. Common allergic reactions include eczema, hives, hay fever, asthma, food allergies, and reactions to insect venom, such as that from wasps and bees. Mild allergies, such as hay fever, are widespread and cause symptoms like allergic conjunctivitis, itching, and a runny nose. Similarly, asthma, a condition in which allergy plays a significant role, is also common. In some individuals, severe allergic reactions to environmental or dietary allergens, or to medications, can occur. These reactions may lead to life-threatening anaphylaxis and, in extreme cases, death. Various diagnostic tests are available to identify allergic conditions. These include skin testing, where the skin is exposed to known allergens to observe reactions, and blood tests to measure the presence and levels of allergen-specific IgE antibodies. Treatments for allergies include avoiding allergens, using antihistamines, steroids, or other oral medications, undergoing immunotherapy to desensitize the immune response to allergens, and employing targeted therapies. The concept of allergy was first defined in the early 1900s. Over time, it has evolved into a broader understanding of various disease mechanisms associated with dysregulated immune system activation. The study of allergy advanced significantly in the 1960s with the discovery of immunoglobulin E (IgE) by Kimishige Ishizaka. The development of allergic responses occurs in two phases: the acute phase and the late-phase reaction. The body’s response depends on the phase and the progression of chemical mediators involved. The causes of allergies can be categorized into host factors and environmental factors. Host factors, such as genetic predisposition, play a significant role, as allergies often run in families. Environmental factors vary depending on the living environment. Allergies are more prevalent in industrialized countries compared to traditional or agricultural societies. Additionally, urban populations exhibit higher rates of allergic diseases compared to rural populations. It is essential to differentiate allergic responses from other similar conditions, such as vasomotor rhinitis. Accurate diagnosis ensures that patients receive the most appropriate treatment. Allergies can affect various organ systems differently. Depending on the severity, they may cause skin reactions, bronchoconstriction, swelling (edema), low blood pressure (hypotension), coma, and even death. The primary approach to treating allergic responses is pharmacotherapy. Common methods include immunotherapy, which involves desensitization or hyposensitization, and enzyme-potentiated desensitization. Once allergies have developed, managing them and carefully avoiding known triggers can help prevent future allergic reactions.
